principles.text: In a crisis, trust investors' actions over press narratives: the partners' warning was a good-faith attempt to help founders.
principles.quote: I was there, I looked in the partners’ eyes, they weren’t bluffing. They were trying to help us.

principles.text: Being wrong about a warning doesn't make the warning bad; act on the best information you have and be glad the worst case didn't happen.
principles.quote: That being said, I am glad that presentation ended up being wrong, just as I am glad the Cuban Missile Crisis did not turn into a full-blown nuclear war.

principles.text: Investors who share proprietary knowledge and tactical instructions with portfolio CEOs are giving founders an edge in a downturn.
principles.quote: I don’t see how Sequoia’s efforts to communicate a (somewhat sanitized) version of the knowledge they had to their portfolio CEOs, and to provide actionable tactical instructions to us, could be perceived of as anything but good faith.

principles.text: Context gets lost over time; judging a decision in hindsight, without the fear and uncertainty of the moment, distorts the story.
principles.quote: I am of the opinion that some of the context of that particular event has been lost.

summary: Dalton Caldwell recounts attending Sequoia's 2008 'RIP Good Times' meeting as a portfolio CEO, weeks after Lehman collapsed. He argues the warning was sincere, not manipulative, and that the financial system was in a Cuban Missile Crisis moment. Mostly historical perspective with light lessons on crisis response.
title: Why Sequoia's 'RIP Good Times' warning was good faith, not fearmongering
